title: Neutropenic Diet in Pediatric Subjects: Health Outcomes and Possible Risks
content: The neutropenic diet (ND), also called a low-bacterial or low-microbial diet, is widely used in pediatric oncology and hematology to reduce the risk of presumed foodborne infection. Practices vary among centers, and its effectiveness remains debated. This narrative review aimed to assess the ND’s effectiveness, feasibility, health outcomes, and risks in pediatric hematologic and oncologic populations. Available pediatric evi-dence has not established a consistent infection-prevention benefit over standard food safety practices. Evidence remains limited, and findings in adults, including high-risk patients, cannot be directly generalized to children. The review also identifies potential costs of restrictive diets. Excluding foods such as fresh produce and limiting dietary variety may reduce palatability and energy intake, compromise nutrient and fiber in-take, and affect nutritional status. Dietary restrictions may burden families and inter-fere with children’s food preferences and social experiences. Possible effects on the gut microbiome and intestinal barrier warrant further study; current evidence does not establish these as clinical outcomes of ND in children. Overall, routine ND use in pedi-atric patients is not supported by evidence of superior infection prevention and may impose avoidable nutritional and psychosocial burdens. The review favors careful food handling and hygiene, alongside adequate intake and individualized nutritional sup-port, over blanket food-group exclusions. Clinicians should consider treatment, neu-tropenia duration and severity, nutritional status, and family context. Patients at par-ticularly high risk, including some undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or experiencing prolonged neutropenia, may need tailored precautions. Further pedi-atric research is needed to clarify benefits, risks, and the appropriate duration of any restrictions.
